atoms.canonical_statement: The 2026 Standards of Care chapter provides current clinical practice recommendations for pharmacologic approaches to glycemic treatment in diabetes.
The ADA Professional Practice Committee for Diabetes, an interprofessional expert committee, is responsible for updating the Standards of Care annually or more frequently when warranted.
The chapter covers pharmacologic treatment of adults with type 1 and type 2 diabetes, additional recommendations applicable to all people with diabetes, and special circumstances and populations.
The chapter directs readers to the Standards introduction and methodology for the evidence-grading system and the full Professional Practice Committee roster.
Treat most adults with type 1 diabetes with continuous subcutaneous insulin infusion or multiple daily doses of prandial and basal insulin.
For most adults with type 1 diabetes, prefer insulin analogs or inhaled insulin over injectable human insulins to minimize hypoglycemia risk.

Most adults with type 1 diabetes should receive individualized education to match mealtime insulin to carbohydrate and, when relevant, fat and protein intake and to adjust correction doses for glycemia, glycemic trends, sick days, and anticipated physical activity.

Reevaluate insulin treatment plans and insulin-taking behaviors at regular intervals, such as every 3–6 months, and adjust them for factors affecting treatment choice and individualized glycemic goals.

In type 1 diabetes, absent or near-absent beta-cell function makes insulin essential; insulin deficiency can cause hyperglycemia, hypertriglyceridemia, ketoacidosis, and life-threatening tissue catabolism.

A meta-analysis summarized by the chapter found continuous subcutaneous insulin infusion produced a modest A1C advantage over injection therapy of about 0.30 percentage points (95% CI 0.02 to 0.58 percentage points lower).

Continuous subcutaneous insulin infusion uses only rapid- or short-acting insulin, so interruption of delivery can quickly cause metabolic decompensation and requires education on pump failure and backup insulin.

Figure 9.1 compares type 1 diabetes insulin-delivery approaches across flexibility, hypoglycemia risk, and cost, placing automated insulin delivery at the high-flexibility/high-cost end and simpler injection regimens at lower flexibility and lower cost.

Table 9.1 compares type 1 diabetes insulin plans by timing and distribution, advantages, disadvantages, and dose-adjustment logic, including flexible basal-bolus plans, less flexible multidose plans, and pump-based approaches.

The chapter describes automated insulin delivery systems as the preferred insulin-delivery method for many adults with type 1 diabetes who can use them safely, with trial and real-world evidence showing improved time in range, A1C, and hypoglycemia outcomes.
The chapter reports severe hypoglycemia rates in the DCCT of 62 versus 19 episodes per 100 patient-years for intensive versus conventional therapy during approximately 6 years of follow-up.

The chapter summarizes DCCT evidence in which intensive therapy achieved a mean A1C of about 7.3% versus 9.1% with conventional therapy and reduced microvascular complications by roughly 50%, at the cost of more severe hypoglycemia.
Prandial insulin timing should be individualized to insulin formulation pharmacokinetics, premeal glucose, anticipated carbohydrate intake, glycemic trends, physical activity, and sick-day needs.
Roughly 30–50% of total daily insulin is generally supplied as basal insulin in type 1 diabetes, with the remainder used for prandial and correction needs.

Total daily insulin requirements in adults with type 1 diabetes commonly range from 0.4 to 1 unit/kg/day; a metabolically stable adult may start near 0.5 units/kg/day, while newly diagnosed adults commonly require about 0.2 to 0.6 units/kg/day.

Typical multidose type 1 diabetes plans combine prandial insulin with longer-acting basal insulin, with basal dosing aimed at overnight and fasting glucose and prandial dosing aimed at postprandial excursions.

Figure 9.2 provides a practical initiation and titration pathway for multidose insulin in type 1 diabetes, linking basal-prandial balance, CGM or SMBG review, hypoglycemia timing, and overbasalization signals to dose adjustment.

Pancreas or islet transplantation can normalize glucose and mitigate microvascular complications but requires lifelong immunosuppression, so beta-cell replacement is reserved for selected people with severe metabolic complications and/or kidney transplantation needs.

The chapter notes that donislecel, an allogeneic islet cell therapy approved in the United States in 2023, is indicated for selected adults with type 1 diabetes who cannot meet A1C goals because of recurrent severe hypoglycemia despite intensive management and education.
Figure 9.3 summarizes indications for pancreas and islet transplantation by kidney function, metabolic complications, surgical risk, metabolic need, and patient choice.

Concentrated insulins reduce injection volume; U-300 glargine and U-200 degludec are threefold and twofold concentrated relative to U-100, and U-500 regular insulin requires dedicated U-500 delivery devices to reduce dosing errors.

Inhaled insulin has a faster onset and shorter duration than injected rapid-acting analog insulin, but the chapter warns about reduced FEV1, contraindicates it in chronic lung disease, discourages it in current or recent smokers, and requires spirometry before and after initiation.

Use person-centered shared decision-making to select glucose-lowering medications for adults with type 2 diabetes, considering efficacy, cardiovascular and kidney effects, weight, other comorbidities, hypoglycemia, cost and access, adverse reactions, tolerability, and individual preferences.
Consider initial combination therapy in adults with type 2 diabetes to shorten the time to individualized glycemic goals.

For adults with type 2 diabetes and established or high-risk ASCVD, include medications with demonstrated cardiovascular event reduction, such as a GLP-1 receptor agonist and/or SGLT2 inhibitor, irrespective of A1C.

For adults with type 2 diabetes and heart failure with reduced or preserved ejection fraction, use an SGLT2 inhibitor for glycemic management and prevention of heart-failure hospitalization, irrespective of A1C.

For adults with type 2 diabetes, obesity, and symptomatic HFpEF, include a dual GIP and GLP-1 receptor agonist with demonstrated benefit for heart-failure symptoms and reduction in heart-failure events, irrespective of A1C.

For adults with type 2 diabetes, obesity, and symptomatic HFpEF, include a GLP-1 receptor agonist with demonstrated benefit for heart-failure symptoms and/or reduction in heart-failure events, irrespective of A1C.

For adults with type 2 diabetes and CKD with confirmed eGFR 20–60 mL/min/1.73 m² and/or albuminuria, use an SGLT2 inhibitor or GLP-1 receptor agonist with demonstrated benefit for glycemic management, slowing CKD progression, and reducing cardiovascular events, irrespective of A1C; SGLT2 inhibitor glycemic efficacy is reduced when eGFR is below 45 mL/min/1.73 m².

For adults with type 2 diabetes and advanced CKD with eGFR below 30 mL/min/1.73 m², prefer a GLP-1 receptor agonist for glycemic management because of lower hypoglycemia risk and cardiovascular event reduction; GLP-1–based therapy not dependent on kidney clearance can be initiated or continued during dialysis for cardiovascular and mortality benefit.

For adults with type 2 diabetes, MASLD, and overweight or obesity, consider a GLP-1 receptor agonist with demonstrated MASH benefit or a dual GIP and GLP-1 receptor agonist with potential MASH benefit for glycemic management and as an adjunct to weight-loss interventions.

Figure 9.4 separates type 2 diabetes medication selection into mitigation of cardiorenal complications and achievement of weight and glycemic goals, while allowing those goals to overlap in one person-centered plan.

For adults with type 2 diabetes and biopsy-proven MASH or high risk of liver fibrosis by noninvasive testing, prefer a GLP-1 receptor agonist for glycemic management; pioglitazone or a dual GIP and GLP-1 receptor agonist can also be considered for potential MASH benefit.
Consider pioglitazone plus a GLP-1 receptor agonist for hyperglycemia in adults with type 2 diabetes and biopsy-proven MASH or high risk of liver fibrosis because of potential MASH benefit.
Reevaluate medication plans and medication-taking behavior at regular intervals, such as every 3–6 months, and adjust them for treatment-selection factors and individualized glycemic goals.
Do not delay treatment modification, including intensification or deintensification, for adults who are not meeting individualized treatment goals.
When modifying glucose-lowering therapy, consider individualized glycemic and weight goals, cardiovascular, kidney, liver, and other metabolic comorbidities, and hypoglycemia risk.
When starting a new glucose-lowering medication, reassess the need for and dose of sulfonylureas, meglitinides, and insulin to reduce hypoglycemia risk and treatment burden.
Do not combine a DPP-4 inhibitor with a GLP-1 receptor agonist or dual GIP and GLP-1 receptor agonist because the combination does not add glucose lowering beyond GLP-1–based therapy.

For adults with type 2 diabetes who have not achieved individualized weight goals, add appropriate weight-management interventions such as intensified lifestyle treatment, structured programs, pharmacotherapy, or metabolic surgery.

Consider insulin regardless of background glucose-lowering therapy or diabetes duration when adults with type 2 diabetes have symptomatic hyperglycemia, A1C above 10% (>86 mmol/mol), or blood glucose at least 300 mg/dL (≥16.7 mmol/L).
For adults with type 2 diabetes without severe hyperglycemia or hyperglycemic crisis, prefer GLP-1–based therapy to insulin for initial or add-on glucose lowering.

If insulin is used in adults with type 2 diabetes, combine it with a GLP-1 receptor agonist, including a dual GIP and GLP-1 receptor agonist, for greater glycemic efficacy and favorable weight and hypoglycemia effects, and reassess insulin dosing when GLP-1–based therapy is added or escalated.

When adults with type 2 diabetes start insulin, continue other glucose-lowering agents unless contraindicated or not tolerated to preserve ongoing glycemic, weight, cardiometabolic, or kidney benefits.

For type 2 diabetes, the chapter uses a person-centered treatment framework that integrates glycemic and weight goals with ASCVD, heart failure, kidney disease, liver disease, hypoglycemia risk, adverse effects, treatment burden, cost, access, and preferences.

In adults with type 2 diabetes and ASCVD, heart failure, or CKD, the treatment plan should prioritize agents that reduce cardiovascular and kidney risk even when additional A1C lowering is not required.
Pharmacologic treatment for type 2 diabetes should begin at diagnosis without delay unless contraindications exist.

Table 9.2 compares glucose-lowering drug classes by glycemic efficacy, hypoglycemia risk, weight effects, major cardiovascular events, heart failure, CKD progression, MASH effects, kidney dosing, and key adverse effects.

The medication comparison table highlights genitourinary infections, volume depletion, ketoacidosis, and rare Fournier gangrene among clinically important SGLT2 inhibitor adverse-effect considerations.

The medication comparison table highlights gastrointestinal effects, gastroparesis concerns, gallbladder disease, pancreatitis warnings, retinopathy monitoring in high-risk patients, and possible effects on oral drug absorption among GLP-1–based therapy considerations.
The chapter notes a potential heart-failure risk with saxagliptin among DPP-4 inhibitors and distinguishes linagliptin as not requiring kidney dose adjustment.
The chapter warns that pioglitazone can cause fluid retention and increase heart-failure risk and should not be used in the setting of heart failure.
In adults without ASCVD, heart failure, or CKD, medication choice should be guided by individualized glucose and weight goals and by other comorbidities such as MASLD or MASH.

Metformin gastrointestinal intolerance can often be mitigated with gradual dose titration, extended-release formulations, and administration with food; long-term use can contribute to vitamin B12 deficiency and warrants monitoring when clinically appropriate.

Metformin remains a commonly used, effective, inexpensive, and widely available treatment when no comorbidity-driven drug choice supersedes it; the chapter describes neutral weight effects and low intrinsic hypoglycemia risk.

The insulin intensification pathway emphasizes evaluating overbasalization and adding prandial insulin or other adjunctive therapy rather than continuing to increase basal insulin when fasting glucose is controlled but overall glycemia remains above goal.

When basal insulin is initiated for type 2 diabetes, Figure 9.5 gives an example starting dose of 10 units/day or 0.1–0.2 units/kg/day, followed by fasting-glucose–directed titration and dose reduction for unexplained hypoglycemia.

For metformin and kidney function, the chapter states that it should not be initiated when eGFR is below 45 mL/min/1.73 m², dosing should be reassessed if eGFR falls below 45, and therapy should be stopped when eGFR is below 30 mL/min/1.73 m².

GLP-1 receptor agonists retain glucose-lowering efficacy across kidney function, while SGLT2 inhibitors can generally be initiated when eGFR is above 20 mL/min/1.73 m² but provide less glycemic lowering at lower eGFR.

The chapter summarizes GRADE evidence in a relatively short-duration type 2 diabetes cohort without established cardiovascular disease, reporting fewer cardiovascular events with liraglutide than with comparator therapies (hazard ratio 0.7, 95% CI 0.6–0.9) but no significant differences in MACE, heart-failure hospitalization, or cardiovascular death.
Include healthy behaviors, diabetes self-management education and support, avoidance of therapeutic inertia, and social determinants of health as essential components of glucose-lowering management.

Recommend continuous glucose monitoring at diabetes onset and thereafter for adults on insulin, on noninsulin therapies that can cause hypoglycemia, or on any diabetes treatment where CGM aids management; choose the device and method according to individual circumstances, preferences, and needs.

Monitor for overbasalization during insulin therapy using bedtime-to-morning or postprandial-to-preprandial glucose differentials, hypoglycemia, and high glycemic variability, and promptly reevaluate therapy when overbasalization is suspected.
Offer automated insulin delivery systems to adults with type 1 or type 2 diabetes who use insulin, according to the person’s or caregiver’s needs and preferences.

Prescribe glucagon for all individuals taking insulin or at high risk for hypoglycemia; ensure support persons know where it is and how to administer it, and prefer preparations that do not require reconstitution.
Routinely assess people with diabetes for financial barriers and use collaborative strategies to reduce costs and improve access to evidence-based care.

For adults with diabetes and cost-related barriers, consider lower-cost glucose-lowering medications such as metformin, sulfonylureas, thiazolidinediones, and human insulin while accounting for hypoglycemia, weight gain, cardiovascular and kidney events, and other adverse effects.

Continuous glucose monitoring improves glycemic outcomes such as A1C and time in range and reduces hypoglycemia in adults using insulin or other therapies that can cause hypoglycemia, according to evidence summarized by the chapter.

Table 9.3 reports U.S. median monthly 30-day acquisition costs for noninsulin glucose-lowering medications at maximum approved daily doses, using average wholesale price and National Average Drug Acquisition Cost data current to 15 July 2025.
The cost tables are acquisition-price references rather than estimates of an individual patient’s out-of-pocket cost and can become outdated as prices and market conditions change.
Table 9.4 reports U.S. median acquisition costs for insulin products per 1,000 units using average wholesale price and National Average Drug Acquisition Cost data current to 15 July 2025.

Glucocorticoid-associated hyperglycemia is driven by dose and pharmacokinetic pattern, so glucose-lowering therapy should be coordinated with steroid timing and reassessed as glucocorticoid doses change.
Do not recommend non-FDA-approved compounded glucose-lowering products because their content, safety, quality, and effectiveness are uncertain.
When a glucose-lowering medication is unavailable during a shortage, switch to an FDA-approved medication with similar efficacy when appropriate.
The chapter distinguishes FDA-approved glucose-lowering products from non-FDA-approved compounded products and advises use of approved alternatives during shortages when clinically appropriate.
After a medication shortage resolves, reassess whether to resume the original FDA-approved glucose-lowering product.
For individuals with diabetes and childbearing potential, counsel about contraception and about the potential effect of glucose-lowering medications on contraceptive effectiveness.

Use person-centered preconception planning for individuals with diabetes and childbearing potential, including glycemic goals, timing of discontinuation of noninsulin glucose-lowering medications, and optimal glycemic management for pregnancy.

For hyperglycemia associated with immunotherapy, assess the immediate need for insulin because of diabetic ketoacidosis risk while evaluating the cause, and use close monitoring, education, and dose adjustment when insulin is started.
Use metformin as first-line treatment for hyperglycemia caused by mTOR inhibitors.
Use metformin as first-line treatment for hyperglycemia caused by PI3K-alpha inhibitors such as alpelisib or inavolisib.
Reserve insulin for severe hyperglycemia or hyperglycemic crisis caused by PI3K inhibitors because insulin may affect PI3K inhibitor efficacy.
For glucocorticoid-associated hyperglycemia, adjust or add glucose-lowering medication to match the glucocorticoid treatment plan and reassess frequently.
For posttransplantation diabetes mellitus or preexisting type 2 diabetes, prefer insulin for postoperative hyperglycemia and consider a DPP-4 inhibitor for mild hyperglycemia.
For posttransplantation diabetes mellitus or preexisting type 2 diabetes, use noninsulin pharmacotherapy for long-term management, with medication selection potentially varying by transplanted organ.

For posttransplantation diabetes mellitus or preexisting type 2 diabetes, consider a GLP-1 receptor agonist for long-term treatment to obtain cardiovascular, kidney, weight, liver, and other cardiometabolic benefits.
If individualized long-term glycemic goals cannot be achieved or maintained with noninsulin pharmacotherapy after transplantation, consider adding insulin.

Educate people at risk for diabetic ketoacidosis who are treated with SGLT inhibition about ketoacidosis risk, signs, mitigation, and management; provide ketone-measurement tools such as serum beta-hydroxybutyrate and discourage a ketogenic eating pattern.

Because GLP-1–based therapies slow gastric emptying most strongly at initiation and dose escalation, the chapter warns that they may alter absorption of oral medications, including oral contraceptives.

Immune checkpoint inhibitor–associated autoimmune diabetes is reported to occur in approximately 1% or less of treated patients and can appear from about 1 week to 12 months after treatment begins, often with rapid severe hyperglycemia or diabetic ketoacidosis requiring insulin.

The chapter reports that tirzepatide can reduce oral contraceptive exposure during periods of greatest gastric-emptying effect and advises a second contraceptive method until the maintenance tirzepatide dose has been used for at least 4 weeks after initiation or dose escalation.

PI3K-alpha inhibitor therapy is associated with hyperglycemia in roughly 60% of treated individuals, usually within the first 2 weeks, with greater risk in people who have preexisting dysglycemia, BMI above 25 kg/m², or age above 65 years.

For posttransplantation diabetes, the chapter emphasizes postoperative insulin when needed and later individualized noninsulin therapy that accounts for organ type, interactions with immunosuppressants, kidney function, cardiovascular risk, and weight.
In type 2 diabetes treated with SGLT inhibition, the chapter reports diabetic ketoacidosis incidence of about 0.6–4.9 events per 1,000 person-years.

SGLT inhibitor–associated diabetic ketoacidosis is reported in about 4% of people with type 1 diabetes, with risk 5–17 times higher than in untreated type 1 diabetes; SGLT2 inhibitors are not approved for type 1 diabetes in the United States.

SGLT inhibitor–associated diabetic ketoacidosis may occur with glucose below typical hyperglycemic thresholds; the chapter notes that up to one third of cases have glucose below 200 mg/dL and one study found 71% at or below 250 mg/dL.
